title: Limits at Infinity and Asymptotes
lead: This section asks what a function does as x grows without bound in either direction. It defines limits at infinity, informally and formally, with the horizontal and oblique asymptotes they give, works out the end behavior of polynomial, rational, radical and transcendental functions, and gathers every tool so far into a strategy for drawing the graph of a function.
objectives: Calculate the limit of a function as $x$ increases or decreases without bound.
Recognize a horizontal asymptote on the graph of a function.
Estimate the end behavior of a function as $x$ increases or decreases without bound.
Recognize an oblique asymptote on the graph of a function.
Analyze a function and its derivatives to draw its graph.
summary_html:
• The limit of $\kf(x)$ is $\kL$ as $x\to \infty$ (or as $x\to-\infty)$ if the values $\kf(x)$ become arbitrarily close to $\kL$ as $x$ becomes sufficiently large.
  • The limit of $\kf(x)$ is $\infty$ as $x\to \infty$ if $\kf(x)$ becomes arbitrarily large as $x$ becomes sufficiently large. The limit of $\kf(x)$ is $-\infty$ as $x\to \infty$ if $\kf(x)\lt 0$ and $|\kf(x)|$ becomes arbitrarily large as $x$ becomes sufficiently large. We can define the limit of $\kf(x)$ as $x$ approaches $-\infty$ similarly.
  • For a polynomial function $p(x)={a}_{n}{x}^{n}+{a}_{n-1}{x}^{n-1}+\ldots+{a}_{1}x+{a}_{0},$ where ${a}_{n}\ne 0,$ the end behavior is determined by the leading term ${a}_{n}{x}^{n}.$ If $n\ne 0,$ $p(x)$ approaches $\infty$ or $-\infty$ at each end.
  • For a rational function $\kf(x)=\frac{p(x)}{q(x)},$ the end behavior is determined by the relationship between the degree of $p$ and the degree of $q.$ If the degree of $p$ is less than the degree of $q,$ the line $y=0$ is a horizontal asymptote for $\kf.$ If the degree of $p$ is equal to the degree of $q,$ then the line $y=\frac{{a}_{n}}{{b}_{n}}$ is a horizontal asymptote, where ${a}_{n}$ and ${b}_{n}$ are the leading coefficients of $p$ and $q,$ respectively. If the degree of $p$ is greater than the degree of $q,$ then $\kf$ approaches $\infty$ or $-\infty$ at each end.

exercises.prompt: Evaluate $\lim_{x\to-\infty}(3+\frac{4}{x})$ and $\lim_{x\to \infty}(3+\frac{4}{x}).$ Determine the horizontal asymptotes of $f(x)=3+\frac{4}{x},$ if any.

answer.solution: Both limits are $3.$ The line $y=3$ is a horizontal asymptote.

exercises.prompt: Use the formal definition of limit at infinity to prove that $\lim_{x\to \infty}(3-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})=3.$

answer.solution:
Let $\varepsilon \gt 0.$ Let $N=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon}}.$ Therefore, for all $x\gt N,$ we have

$|3-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}-3|=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\lt \frac{1}{{N}^{2}}=\varepsilon$

Therefore, $\lim_{x\to \infty}(3-1/{x}^{2})=3.$

exercises.prompt: Use the formal definition of infinite limit at infinity to prove that $\lim_{x\to \infty}3{x}^{2}=\infty.$

answer.solution: Let $M\gt 0.$ Let $N=\sqrt{\frac{M}{3}}.$ Then, for all $x\gt N,$ we have $3{x}^{2}\gt 3{N}^{2}=3{(\sqrt{\frac{M}{3}})}^{2}{}^{2}=\frac{3M}{3}=M$<sup class="fn" data-note="c-cp22-exponent"></sup>

Consider the function $f(x)=5-{x}^{2/3}.$ Determine the point on the graph where a cusp is located. Determine the end behavior of $f.$

answer.hint: A function $f$ has a cusp at a point $a$ if $f(a)$ exists, $f'(a)$ is undefined, one of the one-sided limits as $x\to a$ of $f'(x)$ is $+\infty,$ and the other one-sided limit is $-\infty.$
answer.solution: The function $f$ has a cusp at $(0,5)$ $\lim_{x\to {0}^{-}}{f}^{'}(x)=\infty,$ $\lim_{x\to {0}^{+}}{f}^{'}(x)=-\infty.$ For end behavior, $\lim_{x\to \pm \infty}f(x)=-\infty.$

For $f(x)=\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}$ to have an asymptote at $y=2$ then the polynomials $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ must have what relation?

answer.solution: Since $f$ is a ratio of polynomials, its end behavior is decided by their degrees. It has the horizontal asymptote $y=2$ exactly when $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ have the same degree and the ratio of their leading coefficients is $2:$ if $P(x)=a_{n}x^{n}+\cdots$ and $Q(x)=b_{n}x^{n}+\cdots,$ then $\frac{a_{n}}{b_{n}}=2.$ If the degree of $P$ were less, the asymptote would be $y=0;$ if greater, there would be no horizontal asymptote.

exercises.prompt: For $f(x)=\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}$ to have an asymptote at $x=0,$ then the polynomials $P(x)$ and $Q(x).$ must have what relation?
If ${f}^{'}(x)$ has asymptotes at $y=3$ and $x=1,$ then $f(x)$ has what asymptotes?

answer.solution: None is guaranteed. $\lim_{x\to\pm\infty}f'(x)=3$ means $f$ grows like $3x,$ so $f$ has no horizontal asymptote, and it has an oblique asymptote $y=3x+b$ only if $f(x)-3x$ approaches a limit $b.$ And $f'(x)\to\pm\infty$ as $x\to 1$ does not make $f$ itself unbounded there. For example, $f(x)=3x+3\sqrt[3]{x-1}$ has $f'(x)=3+\frac{1}{(x-1)^{2/3}},$ whose graph has the asymptotes $y=3$ and $x=1,$ yet $f$ is continuous at $1$ and $f(x)-3x=3\sqrt[3]{x-1}\to\pm\infty,$ so $f$ has no asymptote at all.

exercises.prompt: Both $f(x)=\frac{1}{(x-1)}$ and $g(x)=\frac{1}{{(x-1)}^{2}}$ have asymptotes at $x=1$ and $y=0.$ What is the most obvious difference between these two functions?
True or false: Every ratio of polynomials has vertical asymptotes.

answer.solution: False. A ratio of polynomials has a vertical asymptote only where the denominator is zero and the numerator is not. $f(x)=\frac{1}{x^{2}+1}$ has a denominator that is never zero, so it has no vertical asymptote; neither has $\frac{x^{2}-1}{x-1},$ which equals $x+1$ except at $x=1,$ where it has a hole.
